item.passage:
For most of the history of archaeology, a broken cooking pot told researchers about the people who made it but very little about what they ate. The shape of a vessel suggested its use, yet a jar shaped for storing grain might just as easily have held oil or water. Over the past few decades, however, chemists have found a way to read the meals themselves.

Unglazed pottery is porous. When food is cooked in it, fats seep into the walls of the vessel, where they can survive for thousands of years, protected from the bacteria that destroy most organic remains. By grinding a small sample of the pot and extracting these lipids, researchers can identify broad categories of food. Animal fats can be distinguished from plant oils, and, using the ratios of carbon isotopes, the fat of cattle or sheep can be separated from that of pigs and even from milk.

The technique has limits. It identifies what was absorbed, not what was served, so a vessel used only once for a lean meal may record almost nothing. And because each pot accumulates residues over its whole working life, the result is an average of many meals rather than a snapshot of one. Still, residue analysis has overturned some long-held assumptions, showing, for example, that dairy products were being processed in parts of Europe centuries earlier than bones alone had suggested.

able to absorb liquid

item.correct_answer: able to absorb liquid
item.explanation: The next sentence explains it: fats "seep into the walls of the vessel".

distractor_rationales.reason: Decoration is not discussed.

distractor_rationales.choice: easily broken when heated
distractor_rationales.reason: Fragility is not the point; absorption is.

distractor_rationales.choice: heavy and thick
distractor_rationales.reason: Weight and thickness are not mentioned.

item.passage:
Most planets outside our solar system have never been seen directly. They are far too dim, and too close to the glare of their stars, to be photographed with current telescopes. Instead, astronomers detect many of them by watching the star itself.

If a planet's orbit happens to be aligned so that the planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a small fraction of the star's light during each crossing. This event, called a transit, produces a slight, regular dip in the star's brightness. The depth of the dip depends on the size of the planet relative to the star: a planet with a tenth of the star's diameter blocks about one percent of its light. The time between dips gives the length of the planet's year.

Transits reveal only a minority of planets, because most orbits are tilted so that the planet never crosses in front of its star from our point of view. The method also favors large planets close to their stars, which produce deep, frequent dips that are easy to confirm. A small planet in a wide orbit may transit only once every few years, and a single faint dip could have other causes, such as a dark spot on the star's surface.

For this reason, a transit is usually treated as a candidate rather than a discovery until it has been observed repeatedly and checked by another method, such as measuring the slight wobble the planet's gravity produces in the star's motion.

choices: They are hidden behind clouds of dust.
Their orbits are tilted away from Earth.

item.correct_answer: They are faint and lie very close to bright stars.
item.explanation: "They are far too dim, and too close to the glare of their stars, to be photographed."

distractor_rationales.choice: They move too quickly across the sky.
distractor_rationales.reason: Speed across the sky is not mentioned.

distractor_rationales.choice: Their orbits are tilted away from Earth.
distractor_rationales.reason: Tilted orbits explain missed transits, not missing photographs.

distractor_rationales.choice: They are hidden behind clouds of dust.
distractor_rationales.reason: Dust is not mentioned.

item.passage:
Students preparing for an examination commonly study a topic in one long session, reading the same material again and again until it feels familiar. Decades of research suggest that this is one of the least efficient ways to learn. Material studied in several shorter sessions, separated by days, is remembered considerably longer than the same material studied for the same total time in a single block. This finding, known as the spacing effect, is among the most consistently replicated results in the psychology of memory.

Why spacing helps is still debated. One explanation holds that when a learner returns to material after a delay, some of it has been partly forgotten, and the effort of recalling it strengthens the memory more than easy repetition does. Another suggests that studying in different sessions links the material to a wider variety of contexts, giving the learner more cues for retrieving it later.

Despite the strength of the evidence, spacing is rarely the method students choose. Part of the reason is that massed study feels more effective. During a long session, material quickly becomes familiar, and that sense of fluency is easily mistaken for learning. Spaced study, by contrast, involves repeated encounters with material that seems half-forgotten, which can feel like failure. Students who judge their progress by how easy studying feels are therefore likely to prefer the very method that serves them worse.
item.prompt: [Academic — Psychology] According to paragraph 1, the spacing effect refers to the finding that
choices: material studied repeatedly in one session is quickly forgotten
students remember more when they study with others
material studied in separated sessions is remembered longer
long study sessions are more tiring than short ones
item.correct_answer: material studied in separated sessions is remembered longer
item.explanation: Material studied "in several shorter sessions, separated by days, is remembered considerably longer."

distractor_rationales.choice: long study sessions are more tiring than short ones
distractor_rationales.reason: Fatigue is not mentioned.

distractor_rationales.choice: material studied repeatedly in one session is quickly forgotten
distractor_rationales.reason: This states only part of the comparison, not the effect itself.

distractor_rationales.choice: students remember more when they study with others
distractor_rationales.reason: Studying with others is not mentioned.

item.passage:
Students preparing for an examination commonly study a topic in one long session, reading the same material again and again until it feels familiar. Decades of research suggest that this is one of the least efficient ways to learn. Material studied in several shorter sessions, separated by days, is remembered considerably longer than the same material studied for the same total time in a single block. This finding, known as the spacing effect, is among the most consistently replicated results in the psychology of memory.

Why spacing helps is still debated. One explanation holds that when a learner returns to material after a delay, some of it has been partly forgotten, and the effort of recalling it strengthens the memory more than easy repetition does. Another suggests that studying in different sessions links the material to a wider variety of contexts, giving the learner more cues for retrieving it later.

Despite the strength of the evidence, spacing is rarely the method students choose. Part of the reason is that massed study feels more effective. During a long session, material quickly becomes familiar, and that sense of fluency is easily mistaken for learning. Spaced study, by contrast, involves repeated encounters with material that seems half-forgotten, which can feel like failure. Students who judge their progress by how easy studying feels are therefore likely to prefer the very method that serves them worse.

choices: Spaced study is effective only for those students who already find studying easy.

Using ease as a guide leads students toward the less effective method.
item.correct_answer: Using ease as a guide leads students toward the less effective method.

distractor_rationales.reason: Spaced study is said to feel hard, not easy.

distractor_rationales.reason: The passage argues ease is a misleading signal.

item.passage:
Before the printing press reached Europe in the fifteenth century, every book was copied by hand. A single copy of a long work could take a professional scribe many months, and books were correspondingly expensive, owned mainly by monasteries, universities, and the very wealthy.

Printing with movable type did not eliminate this cost all at once. Setting a page of type by hand was itself slow work, and a printer had to buy paper, ink, and metal type before selling a single copy. The savings came from what happened after the type was set: once a page was ready, hundreds of identical copies could be produced at little additional cost. Printing was therefore economical only for works that many people wanted to buy. A printer who misjudged demand could be ruined by unsold stock.

This arithmetic shaped what was printed. Early printers favored texts with large and reliable markets, such as religious works, school grammars, and legal handbooks, rather than the new or specialized writing that later generations would associate with the press. Within a few decades, however, the falling price of books had enlarged the reading public, and a larger public made it possible to risk printing a wider range of works. The effect of the press on what people read was thus gradual, and it depended as much on the growth of a market as on the machine itself.

item.passage:
In the 1990s, researchers found that the roots of many forest trees are connected underground by threads of fungus. These fungi, which grow into and around plant roots, receive sugars from the trees and in return supply water and minerals drawn from the soil. Because a single fungus can attach to several trees at once, the forest floor is crossed by a network that links plants of different ages and even different species.

Experiments using labeled carbon showed that small amounts of sugar can pass from one tree to another through these networks. From such results, a popular picture emerged: forests as cooperative communities in which large "mother trees" feed their shaded seedlings and send warnings of insect attack to their neighbors.

Many researchers now regard this picture as running well ahead of the evidence. The amount of carbon transferred in most studies was small, and it is often unclear whether it reached the receiving tree's tissues or stayed in the fungus. Field studies have also been difficult to reproduce, and some were conducted in conditions unlike those of a mature forest. Moreover, the fungi are not neutral pipes. They are organisms with their own interests, and a transfer that benefits one tree may simply be a side effect of the fungus moving resources for its own growth.

None of this means the networks are unimportant. Rather, critics argue, describing them in terms of family care and communication may have shaped what the public believes before the research could settle the question.

distractor_rationales.choice: minerals
distractor_rationales.reason: Minerals flow from fungus to tree.

item.passage:
When two languages come into long contact, they borrow words from each other, but they do not borrow evenly. English, for example, took thousands of words from French after the Norman Conquest of 1066, while French took comparatively few from English during the same period. The difference reflects the social position of the speakers. French was the language of the new ruling class, used in law, government, and fashionable society, and words tend to flow from the language with more prestige toward the language with less.

The borrowings also cluster by subject. Many English words for law and government, such as "court," "judge," and "jury," come from French, while the words for everyday things and close relationships, such as "house," "bread," and "mother," remained English. A well-known illustration is the pairs of words for animals and their meat: the farm animals, raised by English-speaking peasants, kept their English names, "cow" and "pig," while the meat served at noble tables took French ones, "beef" and "pork."

Linguists caution, however, that such neat stories can be overstated. Some of the meat words entered English well after the Conquest, and for a time the French terms could refer to the living animal as well. The pattern is real, but it emerged gradually, over centuries, as the two languages were used side by side.

item.passage:
When two languages come into long contact, they borrow words from each other, but they do not borrow evenly. English, for example, took thousands of words from French after the Norman Conquest of 1066, while French took comparatively few from English during the same period. The difference reflects the social position of the speakers. French was the language of the new ruling class, used in law, government, and fashionable society, and words tend to flow from the language with more prestige toward the language with less.

The borrowings also cluster by subject. Many English words for law and government, such as "court," "judge," and "jury," come from French, while the words for everyday things and close relationships, such as "house," "bread," and "mother," remained English. A well-known illustration is the pairs of words for animals and their meat: the farm animals, raised by English-speaking peasants, kept their English names, "cow" and "pig," while the meat served at noble tables took French ones, "beef" and "pork."

Linguists caution, however, that such neat stories can be overstated. Some of the meat words entered English well after the Conquest, and for a time the French terms could refer to the living animal as well. The pattern is real, but it emerged gradually, over centuries, as the two languages were used side by side.
